story.title: Theo and the Glowing Launch Button
story.subtitle: One click, one giant leap.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beep in the Dark (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo had exactly four bricks left to place in his newest Roblox Studio build: a rocket launchpad, copied stud for stud from a video he'd watched three times. It was past ten. His door was shut. His headset sat crooked on one ear.

He clicked **Play** to test the countdown script.

The screen didn't flicker. It went black, then a flat green, the green of an old computer screen that still works but barely. A single word blinked where his rocket used to be: LAUNCH?

Theo frowned. He hadn't coded that.

He clicked it anyway.

The laptop screen stretched like fabric, swallowing the desk lamp's light, swallowing Theo, pulling him through a tunnel of falling green numbers. He landed hard on packed dirt, under a sky full of stars he'd never get in his bedroom.

A silver ball sat on a metal stand nearby, about the size of a beach ball, bristling with four thin antennas like a spider that skipped leg day. It was beeping. Steady. Rhythmic. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

"That's the same beep as my Play button," Theo said out loud, to nobody.

"Good ear," said a voice behind him. A woman in a heavy coat was checking a clipboard. "That's **Sputnik 1**. First man-made thing to ever circle the Earth. We sent it up **October 4, 1957**."

Circle the Earth — Theo filed that one away. "You mean it's going around and around up there, like a marble in a bowl?"

"Exactly like that," she said. "Round and round, forever falling, never landing. We call that an **orbit**."

Theo stepped closer to the silver ball before it was lifted onto the rocket. "It's small."

"About **fifty-eight centimeters** wide," the woman said. "Smaller than your beach ball at the pool. Big enough to change the world."

The beeping, she explained, wasn't a message. It was just a simple radio signal, so plain that regular people with regular radios back on Earth could tune in and hear it themselves. No special equipment. Just a beep, bouncing down from space, proving something was really up there.

Theo grinned. In his own game he'd spent weeks trying to make one sound effect feel important. This one had done it by accident, with four antennas and a sense of humor.

"Can I touch it?" he asked.

"Once it's on the rocket, nobody touches anything," she said. "Rule one of launch day."

The ball was lifted, bolted in, sealed. Somewhere behind Theo a countdown began, in a language he didn't speak but somehow understood anyway. Countdowns are basically the same everywhere.

Then the green tunnel yanked him sideways again, and the launchpad melted into static.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Sputnik 2 and a New Team (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Theo landed next in a cold room full of humming machines, a month deeper into the same green blur.

A dog with sharp, curious eyes watched him from behind a window, sitting calmly in a small harness.

"Her name is **Laika**," said a man adjusting dials, not looking up. "**November 3, 1957.** She's about to become the first living creature to orbit the Earth."

Theo crouched by the window. The dog tilted her head at him, like she was sizing up a new player who'd just joined her server.

"She's... a dog. In space." Theo said it slowly, like saying it twice might make it make more sense.

"The Soviets wanted to know if a living thing could survive a launch and an orbit," the man said. "Laika's flight helped answer that."

Theo didn't ask what happened after. He had a feeling the man wouldn't want to talk about it, and honestly, Theo didn't either. He just pressed his palm flat on the glass, the way you'd fist-bump a teammate before kickoff, and the dog pressed her nose to the same spot from her side.

"Good luck up there," Theo said.

The green tunnel grabbed him again — gently this time, like a loading screen rather than a yank — and dropped him somewhere entirely different: a sunny parking lot outside a brand-new building with fresh paint and a sign that still smelled like glue.

**NASA**, the sign read. Underneath, smaller: **October 1, 1958**.

A man in short sleeves was hanging the second half of the letter S, slightly crooked.

"You're off by like, two inches," Theo said, before he could stop himself.

The man laughed and straightened it. "Rookie mistake. We only just started this agency. Sputnik gave everybody a scare, so the country decided it needed one team, one plan, instead of a bunch of separate ones all doing their own thing."

Theo understood that completely. He'd once tried to build a soccer stadium in Roblox with three friends who each built a different-sized goal, in three different corners, with three different color schemes. Nothing had matched. The whole thing had collapsed into a pile of mismatched bricks until they agreed on one plan and one leader.

"So NASA's like... the team captain," Theo said.

"Something like that," the man said, climbing down the ladder. "Though we've got a lot more rockets than soccer balls."

Theo looked up at the fresh sign, glowing a little in the afternoon sun, and felt the floor tilt under him again as the green tunnel came back for its next delivery.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Belt Nobody Could See (1958)
chapters.text:
The tunnel spat Theo out into a control room jammed with people cheering, papers flying, somebody's coffee tipping over and nobody caring.

A thin, silver rocket shape sat on a screen, climbing a wobbly line upward.

"**January 31, 1958**," a woman said, grinning so wide it looked like it hurt. "**Explorer 1.** Our first **satellite** — something that circles the Earth, the same way Sputnik did. Finally."

Theo clocked the date instantly. "That's after Sputnik. You guys were behind."

"Four months behind," she admitted. "But watch this."

A different machine on the desk was ticking out numbers nobody seemed to expect. The woman's grin faded into something sharper — more curious than happy.

"That's strange," she muttered. "The readings keep maxing out the gauge, then dropping to nothing, then maxing out again."

Theo leaned over the paper. The pattern looked familiar — like the lag spikes in a laggy Roblox server, on, off, on, off, for no obvious reason.

"Is it broken?" Theo asked.

"Or," she said, "there's something out there we didn't know was there."

It turned out to be real: a wide, invisible belt of charged particles — tiny bits of electric energy — looping around the Earth high above the sky, too high to see or feel, found by accident because Explorer 1 happened to fly straight through it.

"We're calling it the **Van Allen radiation belt**," the woman said, "after the scientist who figured out what the gauge was actually showing us."

"So it's like... an invisible ring around the whole planet," Theo said. "A force field nobody built."

"Nobody built it, and nobody knew it was there until a satellite flew through it and got confused," she said. "Space had secrets. We only just started finding them."

Theo thought about every secret room he'd ever hidden in a build, behind walls players never thought to check. Earth had been hiding one in plain sight, in a spot nobody had bothered to look, until something flew through it by accident.

He wanted to stay and watch the numbers some more, but the tunnel was already humming behind him, and the room dissolved into green static before he could ask a single follow-up question.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Two Men, Two Flights (1961)
chapters.text:
Theo landed on grass this time, next to a launch tower taller than anything near his house, and a man in a bright orange suit was climbing a ladder toward a hatch.

"**April 12, 1961**," said a voice beside Theo. It belonged to a technician holding a stopwatch like it owed him money. "**Yuri Gagarin.** About to become the first human being to leave the Earth."

The hatch sealed. The countdown rolled. Fire and smoke and noise Theo felt in his teeth.

Then, quiet.

"How long's he up there?" Theo asked.

"**One hundred and eight minutes**," the technician said. "One full **orbit** — all the way around the planet — then back down."

Theo did the math out loud, the way he did everything out loud when he was thinking. "That's less than two soccer matches."

"Less than two soccer matches," the technician agreed, "to go all the way around the entire world."

Gagarin landed safely, smiling in photos that would later hang in a thousand classrooms, and the green tunnel barely let Theo catch his breath before yanking him to a different launch pad, this one with a smaller rocket and a different flag.

"**May 5, 1961**," said a new voice — an engineer in a headset, chewing gum fast. "**Alan Shepard.** First American in space."

"Wait," Theo said, watching the numbers on a nearby screen. "This flight's way shorter than Gagarin's."

"Good eye," the engineer said. "Shepard went straight up, came straight back down. No full orbit — just up, out past the edge of the sky for a few minutes, then home. We call that **suborbital**. Gagarin went all the way around. Shepard didn't, not yet."

"So it's like... Gagarin scored the full goal, and Shepard just got a really good shot on target," Theo said.

The engineer snorted gum through his nose, which was, Theo decided, the single funniest thing he had seen all night. "Something like that, kid. We caught up fast, though. Give us a minute."

Theo didn't get a minute. The tunnel was already pulling at his sneakers.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Dare and the Secret Designer (1961)
chapters.text:
The next room was a stage, with flags and a podium and a man speaking to a huge crowd, his voice carrying clean across a field Theo couldn't see the end of.

"**May 25, 1961**," read a nearby sign. "President **John F. Kennedy**."

"...land a man on the Moon," Kennedy was saying, "and return him safely to Earth — before this decade is out."

The crowd roared. Theo's jaw actually dropped, a little, in a way he'd deny later if anyone asked.

"He just... said that? Out loud? To everyone?" Theo asked a man standing near him with a clipboard and a pencil stub behind his ear.

"He did," the man said. "Now a few thousand of us have to go figure out how."

Before Theo could ask who "us" was, the green tunnel dropped him somewhere colder and much more secretive: an office with blacked-out windows, and a man bent over blueprints who refused to look up.

"You're not supposed to be in here," the man said.

"Who are you?" Theo asked.

"Nobody," the man said. "Officially, I don't exist."

Theo had definitely never heard anyone say that about themselves before, not even the most dramatic kid in his Discord server. "That's... not a real answer."

The clipboard man from before had followed him in, apparently used to this. "That's **Sergei Korolev**," he said quietly. "Chief designer of the entire Soviet rocket program. His name was kept a total secret, even inside his own country, until after he died in **1966**. The government didn't want anyone to know who to target."

"So he's like a modder who builds the best game on the server," Theo said slowly, "but never once puts his username on it."

Korolev almost smiled at that, just barely, before going back to his blueprints.

The tunnel dragged Theo once more, this time to a sunnier workshop full of massive rocket parts, where a broad-shouldered man with a thick accent was sketching something enormous on a chalkboard.

"**Wernher von Braun**," the clipboard man said. "Built rockets back in Germany, years ago. Now he's leading the team building the rocket that's actually going to get us to the Moon."

"Two different countries," Theo said. "Two secret geniuses. Both just... building the biggest thing they can think of."

"That's the whole race," the man said, "in one sentence."

chapters.heading: Level 6: First Woman, First Walk (1963–1965)
chapters.text:
Theo's next landing spot smelled like jet fuel, and a woman in a flight suit was signing a photograph for a little girl at the fence.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said the clipboard man, suddenly back at Theo's side. "**June 16, 1963.** About to become the first woman in space."

"She used to work in a factory," he added, before Theo could ask. "Now she's about to orbit the Earth **forty-eight times**."

Tereshkova caught Theo staring and grinned. "Something wrong?"

"No," Theo said quickly. "Just — that's a lot of laps."

"Forty-eight," she agreed. "I'll let you know how many I've got left when I land."

She didn't wait for his reply. She walked straight to the rocket like she had somewhere to be, which, Theo supposed, she did.

The tunnel's next stop made Theo's stomach drop in a way that had nothing to do with traveling through green static.

A man in a bulky white suit floated outside a small spacecraft, tethered by a single cord, Earth curving enormous and blue beneath his boots.

"**Alexei Leonov**," the clipboard man said. "**March 18, 1965.** First person to ever leave his spacecraft and float free in open space. We call that a **spacewalk**."

"Is the cord... enough?" Theo asked. The cord looked impossibly thin against all that empty dark.

"It's enough," the clipboard man said. "It's attached to the capsule. He's not going anywhere he doesn't choose to go."

Theo watched Leonov tumble slowly, weightless, grinning through his visor at nothing and everything.

"How long's he out there?" Theo asked.

"About ten minutes," the clipboard man said. "Then back inside, safe and sound."

Ten minutes didn't sound like very long at all, until Theo pictured himself floating outside anything, tethered by one thin cord, with nothing underneath him but the whole planet. Then ten minutes sounded like plenty.

"I wouldn't do that," Theo admitted.

"Most people wouldn't," the clipboard man said. "That's sort of the whole point of doing it first."

Leonov climbed back inside. The hatch sealed. Somewhere, Theo imagined, people exhaled all at once.

The green tunnel swept him away again before he could ask whether Leonov had liked it.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Photo That Changed Everything (1968)
chapters.text:
The tunnel let Theo out somewhere with no floor at all — just a window, and beyond the window, the Moon's gray surface sliding by close enough to touch.

"**December 1968**," the clipboard man said. "**Apollo 8.** First humans to ever orbit the Moon."

Three astronauts floated near the window, cameras in hand, arguing cheerfully about something.

Then one of them went still.

Theo followed his gaze. Over the edge of the gray Moon, impossibly small and impossibly blue, Earth was rising.

Nobody said anything for a second. Not the astronauts, not the clipboard man, not Theo.

"Camera — quick, color film, hurry," said the astronaut, scrambling.

"**William Anders**," the clipboard man murmured, as the camera clicked. "That photo's going to be called **Earthrise**. People are going to hang it on walls for the rest of history."

Theo understood that feeling completely. Every time he finished a build he was proud of, he took a screenshot before touching another brick, just in case the moment never looked quite that good again.

"It's just... Earth," Theo said. "We live there. Why's it such a big deal to see it from here?"

"Because nobody's ever seen their whole home like that before," the clipboard man said. "Every person who's ever lived, right there, in one little blue marble, floating in all that black."

Theo pressed his face near the glass, careful not to actually touch it. The Moon's surface looked close enough to walk on. Earth looked small enough to hold.

"Next time," the clipboard man said, "somebody's actually going to walk on that gray ground down there."

"Who?" Theo asked.

The clipboard man smiled like he already knew, and wasn't telling.

The tunnel pulled Theo in before he could push the question, and the last thing he saw through the glass was Earth, rising.

chapters.heading: Level 8: One Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
Theo's boots hit real ground this time — gray, dusty, crunchy underfoot, like walking on a beach made of flour.

Above him, a rocket the length of a soccer field stacked on end still smoked faintly on a pad miles behind, though Theo had clearly skipped straight to the good part.

"**363 feet**," the clipboard man said, pointing back at where the **Saturn V** had stood before launch. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty. That's what it took to get here."

"**July 20, 1969**," he added, as two figures in bulky white suits bounced across the gray ground ahead.

Theo recognized the moment before anyone said the name. He'd seen the photo a hundred times, on posters, on the cover of a library book he'd renewed twice.

"**Neil Armstrong**," Theo whispered.

Armstrong planted one boot, then stepped down fully, his voice crackling through a radio Theo could somehow hear perfectly.

"That's one small step for man," Armstrong said, "one giant leap for mankind."

"**IT'S REAL**," Theo shouted, and nobody told him to be quiet, because out here, there was nobody around for a few hundred thousand miles to hush him.

A second astronaut bounced down after Armstrong. "**Buzz Aldrin**," the clipboard man said. "Joined him down here. Their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, is orbiting alone up above, in the **command module** — the part of the spacecraft that stayed in space the whole time — named **Columbia**."

"Alone up there? While they're down here?" Theo asked.

"Somebody had to stay with the ship while the other two went for a walk," the clipboard man said.

Theo bounced once, experimentally, on the gray dust, the way Armstrong and Aldrin were bouncing. Low gravity made every step feel like a video game glitch where you forgot to turn off the jump height.

"Between **1969 and 1972**," the clipboard man said, "**twelve** astronauts are going to walk on this same gray ground, across six separate trips."

"Twelve," Theo repeated. "That's basically a whole starting squad."

"Give or take," the clipboard man said, grinning. "With a very strange away kit."

Theo looked up. Earth hung in the black sky above him, small and blue and perfect, exactly like it had looked through that other window. He didn't want to leave. The tunnel, predictably, didn't care.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Flight That Almost Wasn't (1970)
chapters.text:
The next room had no windows at all — just screens, and every single one of them showing numbers that made grown adults go pale.

"**1970**," the clipboard man said, quieter than before. "**Apollo 13.** On the way to the Moon when something went wrong."

"What happened?" Theo asked.

"An oxygen tank exploded," the clipboard man said. "Damaged the spacecraft badly, on the way there. Suddenly getting to the Moon didn't matter anymore. Getting three astronauts home did."

Theo's stomach tightened. This was the part of every story where something bad was allowed to happen.

"Are they okay?" he asked, straight out, because he needed to know before he could listen to anything else.

"They made it home safe," the clipboard man said immediately. "Every single one of them. That's the end of this story, so you can relax into the middle of it."

Relieved, Theo turned back to the screens, where engineers were staring hard at a small pile of spare parts and odds and ends already sitting on board, like a puzzle with no instructions.

"They need to fix an air problem," the clipboard man explained, "using only whatever already happens to be inside the spacecraft. Nothing extra. No trip to the store."

Theo knew this feeling better than almost anyone on Earth. Every time he'd run out of the right block in Roblox Studio halfway through a build, he'd had to solve it with whatever was already sitting in his inventory. "That's exactly like finishing a level when your good pieces glitched out," he said. "You use what you've got. You make it work anyway."

"That's precisely what they did," the clipboard man said. "Spent hours figuring it out with nothing but what was already on board. Then they built it for real, inside the actual spacecraft, piece by piece."

Theo watched the astronauts assemble something clunky and strange-looking, fitting it together by hand, and the room around him finally exhaled.

"Made it home safe," the clipboard man repeated, like he knew Theo needed to hear it twice.

"Made it home safe," Theo echoed, and this time, when the tunnel grabbed him, it didn't feel so rough.

chapters.heading: Level 10: The Handshake in Orbit (1975)
chapters.text:
Theo landed in space this time — properly in space, floating, no gravity at all, two spacecraft drifting slowly toward each other against a wall of black.

One had Russian letters on the side. One had American ones.

"**July 17, 1975**," the clipboard man said. "Last stop. This is where the whole race ends."

Theo watched the two crafts line up, nose to nose, a connector sliding into place with a soft mechanical CLUNK that echoed through Theo's bones even though there was supposedly no sound in space.

"That's called **docking**," the clipboard man said. "Joining two spacecraft together, in orbit."

A hatch opened. An American astronaut reached through into the Russian spacecraft. A Soviet crew member reached back.

They shook hands.

Theo had watched plenty of soccer matches end with a handshake line, winners and losers filing past each other, hands out, respect intact either way. He'd never thought about it meaning much beyond good manners.

This felt different. This felt like the actual final whistle on something that had lasted eighteen years.

"Eighteen years," Theo said slowly. "From a beeping ball, to a dog, to a secret guy who wasn't allowed to have a name, to a guy walking on the Moon in front of the whole planet. And it ends with... a handshake."

"Started as a race," the clipboard man said. "Ended as a team-up."

Theo thought that sounded like the best possible ending to any match he could imagine — two different squads, each playing as hard as they possibly could, finally meeting in the middle once the real work was done.

The green tunnel opened one last time, gentler than ever, and Theo tumbled back through falling numbers into his own dark bedroom, landing soft in his desk chair instead of hard on dirt.

His laptop screen glowed ordinary blue again. His half-finished rocket build sat exactly where he'd left it.

Except for one thing.

A tiny block sat in the corner of his build, shaped like a silver ball with four thin antennas, one he definitely hadn't placed there himself. Underneath it, a small label blinked: **SEE YOU NEXT LAUNCH.**

Theo saved the file. Twice, just to be safe.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a two-player rocket level to finish — and a launch button that might not be done with him yet.

On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it 'a giant leap for mankind.'
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried the astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.

story.title: Maya and the Ship Called Titanic
story.subtitle: A gentle voyage to the biggest ship in the world — and the people who helped each other home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Boat That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, feet drumming the carpet, pencil scratching fast. It was way past bedtime. She wanted one more boat.

She drew a big one. Three tall chimneys. A sharp front, like a shark's nose. She wrote TITANIC across the hull in big wobbly letters.

The pencil line glowed blue.

"Whoa," Maya whispered.

The little paper boat lifted right off the page. It hummed like a kettle and grew bigger and bigger, until a real wooden boat sat glowing on her carpet.

A soft voice came from its bow. "Permission to come aboard, Maya?"

She had drawn boats a hundred times. None of them had ever talked back. She climbed in anyway.

"Where are we going?" Maya asked.

"Back to where the real Titanic began," said the boat. "Belfast, Ireland. The year is 1909."

The window turned to fog, then to gray sky and hammering sounds. When it cleared, Maya floated above a giant shipyard full of sparks and clanging metal. A ship's long metal spine stretched out below, longer than her whole street.

"That spine is called a **keel**," said the boat. "It's the very first part builders put down. Everything else gets built on top of it, like the first line you draw before a whole picture."

Maya spotted a sign nailed to a post. "It says **31 March 1909**," she read. "Is that today?"

"That's the very day workers laid this keel," said the boat. "Good eye."

Maya reached for her pencil, already itching to draw what came next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Biggest Ship in the World
chapters.text:
The boat zoomed forward through swirling fog. "Hold on," it said. "Skipping ahead two years."

They landed by a river packed with cheering people. A huge ship slid down into the water with a giant splash.

"That's called a **launch**," said the boat. "**31 May 1911**. It just means the finished ship touches water for the very first time."

Maya counted the smokestacks poking up from the deck. "One, two, three, four!"

"Good counting," said the boat. "But here's a secret. Only three of those ever had real smoke coming out. The fourth was just for looks, so the ship would seem even grander."

Maya giggled. "A fake chimney? That's sneaky."

"A little bit," the boat agreed.

Later, they floated alongside the finished ship. Maya tilted her head back and back and still couldn't see the top.

"How long is she?" Maya asked.

"About **882 feet**," said the boat. "Picture almost three soccer fields end to end. When Titanic was built, she was the biggest ship anyone had ever floated."

Maya pulled out her sketchbook and tried to fit the whole ship on one page. It didn't fit. She had to tape on a second sheet.

"Even my paper isn't big enough," she laughed.

The boat's little bell chimed, like a laugh of its own.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sixteen Boxes That Should Have Kept Her Safe
chapters.text:
"Come below," said the boat, dipping through a doorway that shouldn't have fit a boat at all.

Inside, Maya saw the ship sliced open like a cake, so she could see every floor at once.

"Look at the bottom," said the boat. "See those walls splitting it into boxes?"

Maya counted along a row. "...fourteen, fifteen, sixteen!"

"**Sixteen compartments**," said the boat. "Each one has its own **watertight** door, which just means water can't sneak through it. If water ever got into one box, the others would stay dry, and the ship would keep floating."

"So nothing could ever sink it?" Maya asked.

"That's what people thought," said the boat, a little quieter. "People even called her 'nearly unsinkable,' which means almost impossible to sink. We'll see how that idea gets tested."

Maya frowned a little. "That sounds like trouble is coming."

"A little," said the boat gently. "But remember, you're safe with me the whole time."

Maya reached out and touched one of the heavy metal doors. It didn't budge.

"Strong," she said.

"Very strong," said the boat. "Now let's go meet the ship on her very first trip."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Away From Southampton
chapters.text:
Horns blasted. Paper streamers flew through the air like confetti snow.

"We've landed in **Southampton, England**," said the boat. "**10 April 1912**. Titanic's very first trip. She's heading across the ocean to New York City."

Maya waved at the crowd, even though nobody could see her.

On the top deck stood a tall man with a white beard and a captain's hat.

"That's **Captain Edward Smith**," said the boat. "One of the most experienced captains in the whole White Star Line. He's sailed more ships than you've drawn boats."

"That's a LOT of ships," Maya said.

The captain gave a calm nod to his crew. The great ship began to move. Maya felt the deck hum beneath her sneakers.

"Where does she go now?" Maya asked.

"West," said the boat. "Out into the cold, deep ocean."

Maya pulled her sketchbook close and drew Captain Smith's tall hat, humming along with the engines as the shore slid away behind them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Something in the Dark
chapters.text:
Four nights later, the ocean turned quiet and still.

"It's so dark," Maya whispered, looking out at black water and a sky full of stars.

"Cold nights like this make icebergs hard to spot," said the boat. "No moon to light them up."

Maya pressed her nose to the rail, watching.

Then, far ahead, something pale slid out of the dark.

"ICEBERG!" Maya shouted, pointing.

Up on the ship, a bell clanged three times. Sailors spun the wheel hard.

At **11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912**, the ship's side scraped against the ice, deep below the waterline.

Maya grabbed the rail. "Are we okay?"

"We're safe," said the boat softly. "We're watching from just above the water, remember? Nobody on our little boat can be hurt."

The scraping stopped. The night went quiet again.

"But the big ship?" Maya asked.

"The scrape let water sneak into more of those sixteen boxes than anyone expected," said the boat. "Let's go see what the crew does about it."

Maya held tight to the rail, brave and curious instead of scared, watching lantern lights begin to move across Titanic's deck.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Calling for Help
chapters.text:
Down in a tiny room, two men sat hunched over a crackling machine.

"Those are the **wireless** operators, **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**," said the boat. "A wireless machine sends messages through the air without any wires at all, like an old-fashioned radio."

Jack's fingers tapped out short beeps. "What's he saying?" Maya asked.

"First he sent the old distress call, **CQD**," said the boat. "Then he tried a brand new one too: **SOS**. Three short beeps, three long, three short. Easy to remember, easy to hear."

Maya tapped her own fingers on the rail, copying the rhythm. "SOS," she whispered.

Up on deck, sailors helped people into small boats hanging off the ship's sides.

"There are only enough lifeboats for about **1,178 people**," said the boat quietly. "Fewer than everyone aboard."

Maya's eyes went wide. "That's not enough boats!"

"You're right," said the boat. "It's one of the biggest lessons this ship ever taught the world."

A woman in a big hat rowed hard at the oars of one lifeboat, calling out cheerfully to keep spirits up.

"That's **Molly Brown**," said the boat. "People later called her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown,' because she rowed and helped and never gave up."

Somewhere above, music drifted across the water, calm and steady.

"Legend says the ship's band kept playing, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**," said the boat. "Nobody's completely sure which songs. But survivors really did remember hearing music, right until the end."

Maya listened to the faint, brave little tune and felt her chest go warm instead of scared.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ship That Came Running
chapters.text:
Hours passed. Maya's boat bobbed gently near the little lifeboats, waiting.

Then, far off, a light appeared.

"That's the **Carpathia**," said the boat. "Another ship. She heard the SOS and raced all night long to reach the lifeboats."

By sunrise, the Carpathia was pulling people up one by one, wrapping them in warm blankets.

Maya watched a small dog get lifted aboard inside someone's coat. "A puppy!"

"A couple of little dogs made it too," said the boat. "Tucked safe the whole time."

Maya smiled, then turned a little serious. "Did everyone get saved?"

The boat's glow dimmed, gentle and honest. "Not everyone could fit in a lifeboat, and the ship was lost that night. It made the whole world very sad. Captain Smith stayed aboard to help others right to the end. But many people were saved, because the Carpathia came, and because people like Molly Brown kept rowing."

Maya was quiet a moment, watching families hug on Carpathia's deck.

"That's good," she said softly. "That they came for them."

"After that night," said the boat, "people made new rules. Every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for every single passenger, and a new ice patrol started watching the ocean, so captains would always know where the ice was."

Maya nodded slowly. "So next time, everyone gets a boat."

"Exactly," said the boat. "Every time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The boat's glow flickered, and fog rolled in once more.

"One more stop," it said. "Far into the future. The year is **1985**."

They sank down and down, through water so dark Maya couldn't see her own hands, until bright lights cut through the gloom below. A small yellow submarine glided past, cameras blazing.

"That's **Robert Ballard**," said the boat. "An ocean explorer. He searched for years, and on **1 September 1985**, he finally found Titanic resting on the sea floor."

Maya peered down. Below them lay the huge ship, quiet and still.

"How deep is she?" Maya whispered.

"About **12,500 feet** down," said the boat. "Deeper than ten tall buildings stacked up. She broke into two big pieces on the way down, resting near a place called Newfoundland, in Canada."

Maya opened her sketchbook, hands a little shaky in the cold dark, and drew the broken shape anyway, because even broken things deserve a careful drawing.

"People still visit her story," said the boat. "Plates, shoes, all sorts of things from the ship are kept safe in museums now, so nobody forgets. There's even a museum shaped like a ship's front, built in **Belfast** in **2012**, right where she was born."

"She came home," Maya said. "Sort of."

"Sort of," agreed the boat. "Speaking of home..."

The fog swirled bright blue, and the cold sea floor melted away. Maya blinked. She was back on her bedroom carpet, pencils scattered everywhere.

The little paper boat lay flat on her sketchbook page again, glowing faintly, then not at all.

Maya looked at her drawing. Beside the big ship she'd scribbled, there was now a tiny lifeboat, sixteen tiny doors along the hull, and a tiny dog peeking over the edge.

"Fair winds," the boat whispered, so quiet she almost missed it.

Maya traced the hull with one finger and climbed into bed, already dreaming of the next boat she'd draw.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Fair winds and calm seas.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow Puddle
story.subtitle: A splashy, colorful bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Puddle Outside
chapters.text:
Ivy was painting big circles on her bedroom floor, blue, then yellow, then purple.

Outside her window, rain had just stopped. A puddle sat on the sidewalk, round and shiny and still.

Ivy pressed her nose to the glass. "Hello, puddle," she whispered.

The puddle blinked back a tiny light. **FLICKER-FLICKER.**

Ivy gasped and ran outside in her socks, paintbrush still in her hand.

A little drop of water popped up from the puddle, round as a marble, and smiled at her.

"Hello, Ivy! I'm Pip," said the drop. "Want to see where rainbows come from?"

Ivy nodded so hard her curls bounced. "Yes! Yes! Yes!"

Pip glowed bright gold. **WHOOSH!** Ivy shrank down, down, down — until the little puddle looked like a whole sunny lake.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Sun Behind, Rain Ahead
chapters.text:
Ivy stood on a cloud of soft mist. The sun was warm on her back.

"Look," said Pip. "Where is the sun, Ivy?"

Ivy turned around and pointed. "Behind me!"

"And where is the rain?"

Ahead of her, tiny raindrops floated like see-through jewels. "Right there!" said Ivy.

"That's the secret," said Pip. "Sun behind you. Rain in front of you. That is how you find a rainbow."

Ivy clapped both hands. "Sun behind, rain ahead!"

"Sun behind, rain ahead!" Pip clapped back, splashing tiny drops everywhere.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
One little raindrop glowed brighter than all the others. **TWINKLE.**

"Can I go inside?" Ivy asked.

Pip smiled. "Sunlight goes inside too. Watch close."

A thin gold beam of sunlight zoomed toward the drop. It dipped and bent, just like a straw looks bent in a cup of water.

"It bent!" Ivy shouted. "The light bent!"

"Water bends light," said Pip. "Every single time, Ivy."

Ivy touched the raindrop's curvy side with one finger. "Like my paintbrush looks bendy in my water cup!"

"Just like that," said Pip, bobbing happily.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Bounce Inside
chapters.text:
Inside the drop, the gold beam zoomed all the way to the back wall.

**BONK!** It bounced, like a ball off a wall.

Ivy giggled and clapped. "Bounce!"

"That's right," said Pip. "Light bounces off the back of the raindrop. Then it turns right around."

Ivy watched the little beam turn and head back the other way. "It's coming back now!"

"Light always comes back home," said Pip softly, "just a different way than it went."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Colors Spill Out
chapters.text:
The gold beam zoomed back out of the drop. It bent one more time.

**SPLOOSH!** Colors spilled into the sky — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple, all in a row.

Ivy gasped. "All the colors came out!"

"Long, long ago," said Pip, "a man named Isaac Newton found this too. He used a little glass triangle called a prism. Sunlight went in white, and all the colors came out the other side, just like this."

Ivy grinned wide. "Just like my puddle!"

"Just like your puddle," said Pip, twirling in the colors.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Why After Rain
chapters.text:
Clouds drifted apart. Sunshine poked through, warm and gold.

"Why do rainbows come now?" Ivy asked.

"Rainbows need two friends together," said Pip. "Sunshine and raindrops, both at the very same time."

Ivy thought hard, tapping her chin. "Like right after the rain stops, and the sun peeks out!"

"Exactly like that," said Pip, bouncing with joy. "You figured it out all by yourself, Ivy!"

Ivy beamed so bright she practically glowed herself. "I'm a rainbow finder."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Painting the Arc
chapters.text:
Pip handed Ivy a tiny paintbrush made of soft mist.

"Paint what you saw," said Pip.

Ivy swooshed red first, then orange, then yellow, green, blue, and purple, in one big curvy arch across the sky.

**SWISH, SWISH, SWISH!**

"That is exactly the right order," said Pip. "You painted a real rainbow, Ivy."

Ivy hugged her misty paintbrush tight. "My favorite colors, all together, all at once."

Pip glowed with pride. "Just like you, Ivy. All your colors together."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Puddle
chapters.text:
**WHOOSH!** Ivy grew back to her regular size.

She was standing by the puddle again, socks wet, curls bouncy, paintbrush still in her hand.

Pip bobbed once more on top of the water. "Goodnight, rainbow finder. Come find me after the very next rain."

Ivy waved both hands. "Goodnight, Pip!"

Inside, Ivy picked up her paintbrush. On her paper, right next to her puddle painting, she painted one tiny rainbow — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

She climbed into bed, her paintbrush resting on the pillow beside her, and her eyes grew heavy and warm.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Dream in every color.

true_facts.text: Sunlight **goes into** a raindrop first.
Inside the drop, the light **bends**, like a straw looks bent in water.
The light **bounces** off the back of the drop.
Then the light **bends again** and comes out, full of colors.
To see a rainbow, the **sun must be behind you**.
The **rain must be in front of you**.
Rainbows need **sunshine and raindrops** together, at the very same time.
That's why rainbows often show up **right after rain stops**, when the sun peeks out.

story.title: Leo and the Sleepy Express
story.subtitle: A glowing owl, a tiny train, and the secrets of sleep

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Hoot Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Leo lined up his trains on the rug. The window was black and quiet. Black and quiet made his tummy feel funny.

He hugged his owl night-light close. Its orange glow felt cozy.

Then the owl blinked, slow and soft. "Hello, Leo," said a gentle voice.

Leo gasped. "Owls don't talk!"

"This owl does," said Hoot. He ruffled his feathers. Tiny glowing tracks curled across the carpet, round and round in a loop.

Leo looked closer. "It's a circle! Like my train track!"

"Just like sleep," said Hoot. "Each night loops around too. Quiet, then wiggly. Quiet, then wiggly. Again and again."

Leo grinned and hopped onto the glowing engine. "Choo choo! Let's loop!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boy with Wiggly Eyes
chapters.text:
The train chugged into a dim, quiet room. A boy lay asleep on a cot. Two grown-ups watched closely.

"Look at his eyes," whispered Hoot.

Leo leaned in close. Under the boy's closed eyelids, his eyes darted fast, side to side. "They're wiggling!" Leo whispered back.

"You found it," said Hoot. "In **1953**, two scientists named **Aserinsky** and **Kleitman** watched eyes wiggle just like that. They named it wiggly-eye sleep, when dreams happen."

Leo pressed his face to the window. "Dreams make eyes dance?"

"They sure do," said Hoot. The train rolled on, leaving the boy to his dream.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Floppy Noodle Sleep
chapters.text:
Next stop: a cozy pillow fort. Leo peeked inside. A sleeping puppy's legs twitched, but its body stayed floppy.

"During wiggly-eye sleep," said Hoot, "the brain works hard, almost like it's awake. But the body goes floppy, like a wet noodle."

"Why floppy?" asked Leo.

"So nobody jumps up and acts out their dream," said Hoot.

Leo flopped his own arms around, testing. They wobbled like spaghetti. "I'm floppy too!"

Hoot chuckled. "Perfect. Floppy keeps dreamers safe and snug."

Leo giggled and flopped all the way onto his seat, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Grow Town
chapters.text:
The train stopped at a sign shaped like a measuring stick. It said GROW TOWN.

"What's this place?" asked Leo.

"The deepest, quietest part of sleep," said Hoot. "Your body uses it to grow bigger and stronger."

Leo stood against the tiny station ruler. He had grown half an inch since last week!

"Deep sleep helped do that," said Hoot. "That's why growing kids need lots of it."

Leo puffed out his chest, proud. "I'm growing while I sleep? Easy job!"

"The easiest job there is," Hoot agreed, smiling.

Leo hopped back on, excited for more sleep already.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Sleepy Clock
chapters.text:
Next, the tracks rolled past a tiny glowing clock, ticking inside a soft, round tunnel.

"What's that clock for?" asked Leo.

"It's your body's own clock," said Hoot. "It tells you when to feel sleepy, and when to wake up."

"How does it talk?" Leo asked.

"With a special sleepy juice," said Hoot. "In **1958**, scientists found it and named it **melatonin**. It whispers, 'nighttime now,' so you start feeling snug and sleepy."

Leo yawned, right on cue. "It's whispering to me!"

"Seems so," laughed Hoot, patting his back gently.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Moonlit Zoo Car
chapters.text:
The tracks curved through a moonlit zoo car.

A dolphin swam by with one eye open. "Why's one eye open?" asked Leo.

"Dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time," said Hoot. "One half rests. One eye stays open to watch for danger."

A giraffe dozed nearby, standing up. "She sleeps so little," said Hoot. "Sometimes less than two hours a day!"

Then a tiny bat hung upside down, snoring softly. "And this sleepy fellow can sleep twenty hours a day," said Hoot. "Champion napper!"

Leo giggled. "I want to nap like a bat sometimes!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Owlet Nest
chapters.text:
The train stopped by a cozy nest. Inside, fluffy baby owls slept in a heap.

"Baby owls, like baby humans, sleep almost all day," said Hoot. "Newborn babies sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours**, and lots of it is wiggly-eye sleep."

Leo peeked closer. "That's way more than me!"

"You're bigger now," said Hoot. "But sleep still has a job for you. It sorts your memories, like tidying a toy box, so you remember what you learned."

Leo thought of his new train trick. "Sleep helps me remember my tracks?"

"Exactly," said Hoot. "Sleep tight, remember right."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home on the Rug
chapters.text:
One more stop: a quiet hallway. A sleepy sheep shuffled slowly, eyes closed.

"Is she dreaming?" asked Leo.

"Actually, no," said Hoot. "Sleepwalking happens during quiet, deep sleep. Not during dreams."

Leo watched a gentle shepherd guide her back to bed. "She's okay though?"

"Safe and sound," said Hoot. "Now, time to go home. People spend about a third of their whole life asleep. That's a lot of important work!"

The glowing tracks curved back toward Leo's rug. The little train puffed to a gentle stop.

Hoot settled back onto the shelf, eyes drooping. "Welcome home, Leo."

Leo snuggled into his blanket, the window not so scary anymore.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Sleep tight, remember right.

true_facts.text: Two scientists named **Aserinsky** and **Kleitman** watched a sleeping boy's eyes wiggle fast under his eyelids in **1953**.
A night of sleep loops around and around, quiet, then wiggly, like a trip around a train track.
During wiggly-eye sleep the brain works hard, but the body goes **floppy** like a wet noodle.
The deepest, quietest sleep helps children **grow** bigger and stronger.
A tiny clock inside the brain tells the body when to feel sleepy and when to wake up.
In **1958**, scientists found a sleepy juice called **melatonin** that whispers 'nighttime' to the body.
Sleep helps tidy up memories, like putting toys back in a toy box, so you remember what you learned.
**Dolphins** sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger.
**Giraffes** sometimes sleep less than **two hours** a day, in short naps while standing.
Some little **bats** can sleep up to **twenty hours** a day — champion nappers!
**Sleepwalking** happens during quiet, deep sleep, not during dreams.
People spend about a **third of their whole life** asleep.
